items.summary: featureTestFiles checks lstat only on the final path, not its parents. Scenario: base tracks test/a.test.mjs, and the feature replaces the test/ directory with a symlink to an outside directory that also contains a.test.mjs. `git diff --name-only` still lists test/a.test.mjs (as deleted), and lstat(top/test/a.test.mjs) follows the parent symlink and reports a regular file. The outside file's content is then copied into the temporary base worktree. SC-2 covers only a test path that is itself a symlink, so this is not a blocking defect, and the impact is low: the head-side run already executes through the link and the base worktree is removed afterwards. Hardening: skip a path when any parent segment under `top` is a symlink, or when realpath(src) is outside `top`.
items.resolution_reason: same as B87 (featureTestFiles parent-symlink lstat); D1

items.summary: overlayFiles copies file mode bits with `statSync(src).mode & 0o777`, which can include group/other write bits from the working tree. This is harmless in a temporary worktree; masking with 0o755 would be tidier.

items.summary: When features.json cannot be written while recording a blocked(eval_error) decision, the io error message tells the user to rerun `harness eval F{n}` to record the status. eval_error verdicts are stored as F{n}-r{k}.eval_error.json and are not picked up by the ES-2 retry path. A rerun therefore evaluates again instead of recording the earlier decision, and that guidance is misleading for this case.
items.resolution_reason: Still true (eval_error has no eval_round retry key, eval-status.mjs:86) but only on a features.json write failure; rerun yields the same blocked outcome at the cost of one adapter call (evidence: lib/eval-status.mjs:86-93)

items.summary: Round numbering continues across contract versions (nextRound is one past the highest existing verdict file), and the previous verdict used for the convergence check may belong to an older contract. After a re-approved contract version, the first interactive eval can already be at k >= max_rounds and go straight to blocked(rounds). SPEC does not say whether rounds reset on a new contract version; this may be worth clarifying.
items.resolution_reason: Rounds are now counted per contract hash (contract_round), so a re-approved contract starts at round 1 (evidence: lib/eval-status.mjs:38-47,120-126 (decideStatus uses contract_round; contractVerdicts filters by hash))

items.summary: decideStatus and record share the eval_error/status-null case only implicitly: `record` returns early for a null status, and `eval_round` is deliberately not set for eval_error. A short comment or a dedicated test for the eval_error blocked → features write failure path would make the ES-2 boundary clearer.
items.resolution_reason: Comment/test-clarity nit

items.summary: The `deps` parameter of evalCommand is split into `{runAdapter, verifyResult}` plus `rest` and then re-wrapped as `deps` for evalAndRecord. This is slightly convoluted; passing a single deps object through would read simpler.
items.resolution_reason: Code-style nit

items.summary: The ES-2 retry path in evalAndRecord runs before the status gate (feature_closed / EVALUABLE check). If an interactive verdict's status was never recorded and a human then set the feature to `skipped` or `todo` (without a new contract version), the next `harness eval` still records that old verdict and overwrites the human-chosen status (e.g. sets `passed`). No adapter is called. Consider allowing the retry only when the status is approved/in_progress, or only when it is still the status from before that round.
items.resolution_reason: Retry path still precedes the status gate (eval-status.mjs:128-135), but needs an unrecorded verdict plus a manual status edit in between; rare, human-induced (evidence: lib/eval-status.mjs:128-146)

items.summary: `--round k` with a gap (e.g. r1 and r3 exist, `--round 2`) is accepted: SC-3 only covers existing rounds. Afterwards the latest eval verdict (r3) differs from eval_round (2), so the next `harness eval` re-records r3's status through the retry path. A cooperative builder is unlikely to hit this, but `--round` could be limited to nextRound() or lower.
items.resolution_reason: --round with a gap is a cooperative-builder non-issue; reporter agrees unlikely

items.summary: decideStatus uses the previous verdict for convergence only when that verdict was `fail`. Run's convergence() compares against the previous failing round's blocking set. After a needs-human or pass verdict with no blocking ids, the comparison resets to the round-1 rule. This cannot happen in practice because those verdicts close the feature, but the two paths are not literally identical.
items.resolution_reason: Theoretical divergence that cannot occur because pass/needs-human close the feature

items.summary: A features.json io failure on a second consecutive eval_error has no retry key: eval_round is not set for eval_error, and no F{n}-r{k}.json exists. A rerun calls the evaluator again (3rd consecutive) instead of re-recording. The outcome (blocked) is the same, but it costs one more adapter call.
items.resolution_reason: Same root cause as B95: eval_error sets no retry key, so a features.json write failure leads to one more evaluator call (same as B95)

items.summary: `evaluate()` and `evalAndRecord` both check for an existing verdict file (`round_exists`). The check in `evalAndRecord` is now redundant with the one in `evaluate`. It could be dropped or shared, but it is not a defect.
items.resolution_reason: Redundant existence check, not a defect

items.summary: `contractVerdicts` reads and parses every verdict file for the feature on each call. In `evalAndRecord`, `evaluate` then calls `contractRound`, which reads them all a second time. This is harmless at small round counts, but `evaluate` could take the already-read list.
items.resolution_reason: Double read of verdict files; harmless at small round counts

items.summary: A verdict file that parses as JSON but has no string `verdict` field is now `state_corrupt` in the run path. Previously `run` never read old verdicts. This is consistent with SPEC E6 and ES-2, but it is new strictness for `run` on hand-edited or legacy files.
items.resolution_reason: Intended strictness per SPEC E6/ES-2

items.summary: `contract_round` is derived from the verdict files and `round` from the run's in-memory counter, so the two can differ in run reports. A short note in the run report may help if the distinction confuses users.
items.resolution_reason: Report wording nit; eval summary already disambiguates contract round vs verdict r<n>

items.summary: `verify.test_count` is unset, so a decrease in the number of tests is not checked (verify warns about this).
items.resolution_reason: verify.test_count is now configured for this repo (evidence: .harness/config.json verify.test_count = "from:commands[0]")

items.summary: evaluate() checks that the verdict file does not exist (refuseExisting) and then writes it with writeJsonAtomic, which renames over any existing file. Two concurrent evals of the same feature could both pass the check, and the second rename would overwrite the first verdict. Creating the file exclusively (open with 'wx', or link/rename-noreplace) would make the no-overwrite rule atomic.
items.resolution_reason: Non-exclusive write, but refuseExisting is re-checked right before writing (eval.mjs:700); remaining window is a sub-second race between two concurrent evals of one feature (evidence: lib/eval.mjs:700,719)

items.summary: harness run keeps its own round counter (e.round starts at 1 per run entry) for max_rounds and the report. The verdict's contract_round is counted from the files on disk. If same-hash verdicts already exist from an earlier eval or run of the same contract, the run gets max_rounds fresh rounds while the verdicts record contract_round > e.round, so the run can exceed max_rounds per contract hash. SPEC §8.8 only covers the re-approval case.
items.resolution_reason: run now carries same-hash verdicts into its round counter (F19) (evidence: lib/run.mjs:1495-1501 (carried = contractVerdicts count), 1236-1238, 1268)

items.summary: contractVerdicts reads every verdict file of the feature, including those of old contracts, so a corrupt verdict from an old contract (or a pre-F18 one) also stops eval and run with state_corrupt. This is stricter than ES-2 (the previous verdict of the current hash) and matches SPEC §7.6 ('hash unknown'), but it cannot be recovered without touching old records.
items.resolution_reason: Documented behavior (SPEC §7.6 hash unknown => state_corrupt); by design

items.summary: In the eval summary, 'round <n>' in the first line is the verdict file number, while the new line shows 'contract round <n>/<max>'. Seeing two different 'round' numbers may confuse users. Consider renaming the first one to 'verdict r<n>'.
items.resolution_reason: Eval summary now labels the file number as verdict r<n> next to contract round (evidence: lib/commands/eval.mjs:34)

items.summary: Carried eval_error verdicts count toward `carried` (the round limit) but add an empty blocking set to history and set carriedPrev to null. The run's evalErrors counter still starts at 0, so consecutive eval_error verdicts from interactive eval are not carried into MAX_EVAL_ERRORS. The contract does not cover this.
items.resolution_reason: Carried eval_error not counted toward MAX_EVAL_ERRORS; outside contract, low impact

items.summary: Before starting a feature, the run re-reads every verdict file of that feature, including files from other contract hashes. A corrupt verdict from an old contract therefore stops the run with state_corrupt, even though it is outside the current hash. This matches the existing E6 behavior of contractVerdicts, but it is stricter than ES-1 requires.
items.resolution_reason: Same documented E6 strictness as B110 (contractVerdicts reads every verdict); by design (evidence: lib/run.mjs:1495, lib/eval.mjs:403-411)

items.resolution_reason: Missing test for security-reviewer adapter_unavailable mid-run; test-coverage nit

items.summary: In the preflight, `callsCli` skips the check when build and evaluate/runAdapter are injected. That is test-only plumbing, and it adds a condition to the run entry point.
items.resolution_reason: Test-only plumbing in preflight condition

items.summary: authStatus treats a settings.json that parses to a non-object, such as `null` or `[]`, as 'not authenticated' with the generic reason. That is acceptable, but it is not distinguished from an absent file.
items.resolution_reason: Non-object settings.json treated as not authenticated; acceptable, reporter agrees

items.summary: verify.test_count is not configured, so a decrease in test count is not checked.
items.resolution_reason: verify.test_count now configured; see B107 (same as B107)

items.summary: For gemini exit codes other than 41 (and for other adapters), runAdapter still puts tail(stderr) into detail as exit_nonzero. If a CLI echoes a credential on some other failure, that text can end up in the run report or verdict. This behaviour existed before F20 and SC-1 only covers the auth decision, so it is not blocking; redacting known auth-variable values from the detail would be a hardening follow-up.
items.resolution_reason: Adapter error detail is redacted by env-value redactor before reaching verdict/state/backlog (evidence: lib/failures.mjs:37-53 redactor; lib/run.mjs:16,466 redactDeep)

items.summary: authStatus trusts any non-empty GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_VERTEXAI / GOOGLE_GENAI_USE_GCA value, including 'false'. That can report 'authenticated' when gemini will actually fail with exit 41. The run then blocks with adapter_unavailable (AC-5), so it fails safe, but the preflight passes when it should not.

Preflight is skipped when both build and evaluate/runAdapter are injected without diagnose. This only affects tests, but a future caller that injects only one of them without diagnose would silently skip the preflight.
items.resolution_reason: Same test-only preflight-skip concern as B121 (same as B121)

items.summary: In runFeatures, the inhibitor is started before `meter = sleepMeter(...)` and `save()`. If either throws (for example a state-file write error), the try/finally that calls inhibitor.stop() and meter.stop() has not been entered yet. The detached inhibitor then stays alive until the process exits. The process-exit hook covers a normal exit, so the impact is small. Moving the `try` up to cover those two lines would close the gap.
items.resolution_reason: Inhibitor started before try (run.mjs:1454-1459); process-exit hook and caffeinate -w/pid watcher still end it (evidence: lib/run.mjs:1454-1463)

items.summary: The AC-4 CLI test only greps lib/commands/run.mjs for the strings `r.sleep`, `system sleep` and `harness run --resume`. It never runs the CLI and never checks the exit code 1 or the stderr text. A regression that broke the printed message would go unnoticed.

There is no test for the post-merge verify path. A sleep during that step throws SystemSleep, and on resume the merge is recognised as done and verified again. That path is implemented, but no test covers it.
items.resolution_reason: Test-coverage gap for post-merge verify sleep path; implemented

items.summary: There are no unit tests for the ticker-gap signal in sleepMeter (the `gapMs` accumulation). All AC-4 tests use the wall-minus-monotonic signal.
items.resolution_reason: Test-coverage gap for ticker-gap signal

items.summary: On win32 the sleep-related tests (AC-1, AC-2, AC-3 exit-case, SC-1, SC-2) return early, so they pass without checking anything.
items.resolution_reason: Platform skip of POSIX-only fake inhibitors; win32 covered by ES-1 test

items.summary: The `verify.test_count` warning still shows in verify output; it comes from project config, not from this change.
items.resolution_reason: verify.test_count warning gone now that it is configured; see B107 (same as B107)

items.summary: The CLI test for AC-4 ('the CLI prints "system sleep" and the --resume hint') only greps lib/commands/run.mjs for the strings. It never runs the command, so it would still pass if the r.sleep branch printed the wrong thing or returned the wrong exit code. The exit 1 that SPEC §8 requires is not asserted anywhere.
items.resolution_reason: Same grep-only AC-4 CLI test (same as B128)

items.summary: The inhibitor is stopped only by the finally block around loop(). It starts before the try, so if save() or sleepMeter() throws in between, the finally never runs. The process.once('exit') handler and caffeinate -w / the linux pid watcher still end it, so no process is left behind. Moving the start inside the try would be cleaner.
items.resolution_reason: Same inhibitor-before-try ordering (same as B127)

items.summary: The inhibitor gets the full process.env (d.env) rather than the adapter env allowlist. It is a fixed system binary, so this is harmless. Noted only for least privilege.
items.resolution_reason: Least-privilege nit for a fixed system binary

items.summary: The linux watcher checks the run pid with kill(pid, 0). If the OS reuses that pid after the run is SIGKILLed, the inhibitor could be kept alive. This needs pid reuse within 1s of death, is not reachable under the cooperative-builder model, and SC-1 only covers SIGINT, where stop() kills the process group explicitly.
items.resolution_reason: PID-reuse race; out of scope (theoretical)

items.summary: No test covers an inhibitor that dies in the middle of a run, the onLost path that SPEC §8 names ('또는 run 도중'). AC-3 only tests the not-on-PATH case and exiting right after start.
items.resolution_reason: Test-coverage gap for onLost mid-run

items.summary: In lib/run.mjs `finish`, resolveItems runs before setStatus. If the features.json write then fails, the backlog items are already marked resolved_by while the feature is not passed. Ordering it after the status write, or making it retryable, would remove the window.
items.resolution_reason: resolveItems before setStatus (run.mjs:1410-1411) is intentional per SPEC §7.7; window only on a features.json write failure (evidence: lib/run.mjs:1408-1411)

items.summary: recordEntries bumps `seen` once per entry. Two entries in the same round that carry the same backlog_id raise seen by 2 but add only one `sources` tag, so seen and sources.length can drift apart.
items.resolution_reason: seen vs sources.length drift on duplicate entries in one round; cosmetic counter

items.summary: An existing item that a later entry hits does not get its priority updated or raised, even when the new entry carries a higher severity. This follows the contract (no retroactive priority), but the evaluator's higher severity is silently lost.
items.resolution_reason: By contract (no retroactive priority)

items.summary: Items without an id get B<n> only in memory when status or the prompt reads them, and are persisted on the next core write. This is consistent and tested. Until that write happens, the id shown in status is not stored anywhere.
items.resolution_reason: Consistent and tested; id persisted on next write

items.summary: lint-contract now reads backlog.json for every run. A corrupt or duplicate-id backlog therefore makes lint-contract exit 2 for contracts that do not use resolves. SPEC §7.7 documents this, but it is broader than the AC-6 wording.
items.resolution_reason: Documented in SPEC §7.7

items.summary: lib/verify.mjs now imports resolveInvocation from lib/adapters/common.mjs, coupling the verify core to the adapter layer. The helper could move to a shared module such as exec.mjs.
items.resolution_reason: Module-coupling refactor preference

items.summary: On Windows the preset executable is resolved with whichWin32 against the parent process.env, while runCommand runs with an allowlisted env. If the allowlist ever drops PATH, the two lookups could disagree.
items.resolution_reason: Hypothetical (allowlist dropping PATH)

items.summary: The pytest parser only matches 'N tests collected'. Output such as '3/5 tests collected (2 deselected)' or a run with plugins that change the summary line gives 'no test count in output'. It fails closed, so this is acceptable, but the SPEC could mention it.
items.resolution_reason: pytest parser fails closed on unusual summary lines; low value

items.summary: preset:node-test runs the project's whole test suite (node --test) just to count tests, once for base and once for head. This is slow for large suites and would recurse if a test itself invoked verify. Consider documenting it, or a --test-only-list approach.
items.resolution_reason: Preset runs suite for count; from:commands[i] (testcount.mjs:54) now avoids the extra run and this repo uses it (evidence: lib/testcount.mjs:54-60)

items.summary: detectPreset matches scripts.test with a substring 'node --test'. It would also match a script like 'echo node --test' or 'node --test-only', which gives a suggestion only and is harmless.
items.resolution_reason: Substring match only affects a suggestion

items.summary: Presets look up bare names (node, go, python) on PATH, the same trust model as a shell test_count. preset:node-test runs whatever `node` is first on PATH rather than process.execPath. That is within the contract, but pinning node to the running interpreter would be a small hardening step.
items.resolution_reason: Hardening nit within contract

items.summary: On Windows, resolveInvocation turns a .cmd/.bat shim (for example python.cmd) into a cmd.exe command string. The arguments are fixed and escaped, so nothing from config reaches the shell. Even so, SC-1's 'without a shell' holds strictly only when the runner is a .exe; the SPEC could mention this.
items.resolution_reason: SPEC wording nit for .cmd shims

items.summary: A value with leading whitespace, such as ' preset:go', is not treated as a preset and runs as a shell command. This matches the existing shell test_count behavior, but a leading-whitespace value that contains 'preset:' could be rejected or warned about to avoid confusion.
items.resolution_reason: Leading-whitespace preset value; matches existing behavior, low value

items.summary: The preset error message includes up to 80 characters of the runner's last stdout/stderr line. That output comes from the project's own runner and env is filtered, so the risk is low. Truncation already limits exposure.
items.resolution_reason: Truncated project-owned output; low risk

items.summary: The F24 tests rely on wall-clock timing: AC-1 uses 12s builder delays and a 0.75× bound, and AC-2, AC-6, AC-7 and ES-2 use hundreds of ms of sleep to order events. They add about 25s or more to the suite and may be flaky on a loaded CI machine. Consider making the ordering deterministic with latches or gates instead of sleeps.
items.resolution_reason: Some ordering now uses latches (startTogether); remaining wall-clock bounds are inherent to the parallelism criterion

items.summary: The `--parallel` value is validated in two places: `parseArgs` in lib/commands/run.mjs and `runFeatures` in lib/run.mjs. The rules could drift apart. Sharing one validator, like `isMaxParallel` in config.mjs, would help.
items.resolution_reason: Duplicate validation; both accept positive integers, no drift today

items.summary: `signal` is either the run's own AbortController signal or the caller's. That choice depends on `maxParallel`, `state.active.length` and whether `outer` exists, which is subtle. Always using `ac.signal` and forwarding `outer` would be simpler.
items.resolution_reason: Readability nit

items.summary: An unused security-reviewer result still costs money. If `unused` reviewer costs are counted in the run total, that is right, but the SPEC does not say so explicitly.
items.resolution_reason: SPEC wording on unused reviewer cost

items.summary: worktreeLock only serializes `git worktree add`; the `git worktree remove --force` and `git branch -D` calls in merge() run under mergeLock instead. With --parallel ≥ 3, a new feature's worktree add can therefore run at the same time as another feature's worktree remove or branch deletion in the shared .git. Git's per-ref locks make an actual collision unlikely, but a transient lock error would show up as blocked('worktree'). One option is to run the post-merge cleanup under worktreeLock too.
items.resolution_reason: worktree remove/prune and branch -D now go through the shared git lock (evidence: lib/run.mjs:149-153 isSerializedGit, 647 gitLock wrapper)

items.summary: In merge(), the builder-changes commit (git add -A / commit in the feature worktree) runs inside mergeLock, so it is serialized behind other features' post-merge verifies even though it only touches that feature's own worktree. This costs throughput, not correctness.
items.resolution_reason: Throughput only, not correctness

items.summary: When the evaluator has a blocking finding, the security-reviewer still runs to completion concurrently and its cost is spent even though the result is recorded as 'unused'. The contract accepts this trade-off, but the spend could be surfaced in the verdict or report.
items.resolution_reason: Unused reviewer cost not surfaced (same as B155)

items.summary: If the evaluator returns ev.error for a critical feature, any error from the concurrently running security-reviewer is silently dropped because only the evaluator error is reported. That matches sequential behaviour (the reviewer would not have run at all), but the reviewer's cost and error are not recorded anywhere.
items.resolution_reason: Matches sequential behavior; low value

items.summary: isSerializedGit covers worktree add/remove/prune and branch/merge/checkout/switch only. Other state-changing core git calls (`git add`, `git commit` and `git reset --hard` in a feature or integration worktree) run outside the lock. This matches the contract's wording, but the SPEC's 'all git calls that change worktrees, branches or merge state' could be read more broadly.

resolveConflict skips the builder when the integration merge into the feature worktree applies cleanly (`files` empty). This can happen if integration moved after the first conflict. The feature is then re-verified and re-evaluated without a builder call and still counts as 'resolved'. The behaviour is reasonable but not described in the SPEC.
items.resolution_reason: Reasonable behavior; SPEC nit

items.summary: The conflictResolution report value for a feature that hit a conflict and was later blocked for an unrelated reason (for example budget or a post-merge verify failure) is 'failed'. The value is derived only from `e.conflictTried` and the final status, so it may overstate that the resolution itself failed.
items.resolution_reason: Report label nuance (failed vs blocked for other reason); low value

items.summary: The AC-4 test records only calls that `isSerializedGit` selects, so it cannot notice a mutating git call that the predicate misses. Its coverage depends on the predicate being complete.
items.resolution_reason: Test depends on predicate completeness; test-style

items.summary: Conflict-marker check after the automatic resolution only scans the files git reported as conflicted; markers the builder leaves or copies into other files are not detected before re-verify/eval (verify/eval would usually catch this).

resolveConflict passes the integration SHA straight to `git merge` without checking it for null; if refs/heads/<integration> cannot be resolved, the argv holds a null element and the failure message is unclear instead of a clean blocked(merge_conflict) detail.

Integration-tip invariance (SC-1) depends on the builder being cooperative. A builder writing through absolute paths into .harness/wt/_integration during resolution is not detected until the re-merge's `git status --porcelain` check, which then throws a run-level worktree error rather than blocking only that feature. This is outside threat model D1.
items.resolution_reason: Outside threat model D1 (reporter states)

items.summary: isSerializedGit also serializes checkout/switch/worktree prune beyond the contract's list; `git reset --hard` and `git commit` in the integration worktree are not under the git lock and rely on the merge lock instead. This is correct today but the two locks are easy to confuse.
items.resolution_reason: reset --hard and commit are now serialized by the git lock (evidence: lib/run.mjs:150-153)

items.summary: F25 blocked (post_merge_verify): verify failed on the integration branch after the merge — verify failed on the merged integration branch; merge rolled back

rewrite the criteria for the feature (new contract version, re-approval)

items.resolution_reason: rescope for F25; feature passed (evidence: features.json F25 status passed)

items.summary: `resolveConflict` catches a conflict-resolution builder that is cancelled or times out only via the generic `fail`/sleep paths. A resumed run from stage 'resolve' with a stale `e.conflict` but no MERGE_HEAD re-merges integration at its new tip, so the conflict files may differ from the persisted list. Behaviour is reasonable but not described in the SPEC.
items.resolution_reason: Reasonable behavior; SPEC nit

items.summary: `validateState` accepts `verifyParallel` only as `{value, auto, cpus}`. An older state file without the field is re-derived on resume, so the applied verify pool size can differ from the one the run started with if the CPU count changed.
items.resolution_reason: Legacy state file edge; low value

items.summary: The conflict-marker check in resolveConflict uses fs.statSync/readFileSync, which follow symlinks. If a conflicted path is a symlink, the core reads the file the link points to, which may be outside the worktree. Nothing is written, so the only effect is a wrong marker verdict. Consider lstat or restricting the check to regular files inside the worktree.

If `git merge --abort` fails in the fail() path, resolveConflict does not check the result. The feature worktree can be left mid-merge while the blocked detail says nothing about it. The integration merge path reports a dirty state in this case; the resolution path does not.

Rows with a missing or unparseable ended_at are silently dropped by `--since` (NaN comparison is false). Rule (a) sorts them as time 0. A hand-edited metrics line that is valid JSON but lacks fields still counts toward `lines` without any warning. ES-1 only covers non-object lines.
items.resolution_reason: Hand-edited metrics lines; low value

items.summary: `harness stats --json` with no metrics files prints the plain text 'no metrics yet' instead of a JSON document. This follows ES-2 literally, but it means machine consumers of --json must special-case this output.
Metrics files grow without bound and `harness stats` re-reads every file on each call. There is no rotation or pruning; --since only filters at aggregation time.
items.resolution_reason: Unbounded metrics growth; small files in practice

items.summary: Rule (c) checks only that features.json contains any standard-tier feature. It does not check whether the builder cost actually came from standard features, so the suggestion can appear when the cost is driven by critical features.
items.resolution_reason: Heuristic suggestion imprecision

items.summary: Timing-based overlap assertions in test/f26-verify-parallel.test.mjs (for example maxOverlap === limit, or the 300 ms and 1000 ms sleeps) can be flaky on a heavily loaded CI machine. The f26 test file took about 59 s to run.

A check that fails while another run is active is retried alone, and 'overlapped' is set whenever any other pool run was live at any point during it. A check that fails on its own merits during a busy period is therefore run twice. That doubles worst-case time for genuinely failing checks (up to 2x step_timeout_sec if a non-timeout failure is slow). This is consistent with the SPEC but worth noting next to B22.
items.resolution_reason: Consistent with SPEC; worst-case latency note

items.summary: Head checks and base vacuity runs share a single pool, and a new criterion's vacuity run only queues after its head check has passed. With a small limit, base vacuity runs can queue behind later head checks. This is harmless for correctness, but overall latency depends on scheduling order.
items.resolution_reason: Latency-only scheduling note

items.summary: Verify still builds the base worktree lazily when test_count is unset. The 'base test count → overlay → vacuity' ordering is then enforced only through the lazy ensureOverlaidBase promise, not through an explicit phase barrier. It is correct today, but the invariant is implicit.
items.resolution_reason: Implicit but correct ordering via lazy ensureOverlaidBase; refactor-only (evidence: lib/verify.mjs:464)

items.summary: The interval-check fixture decides head or base with fs.statSync('.git').isDirectory(). It will misclassify if the test repo is itself created inside a linked worktree or with a different git layout, so the fixture assumes the standard gitRepo() layout.
items.resolution_reason: Test fixture assumption; gitRepo() layout is fixed in tests (evidence: test/fixtures/interval-check.mjs:20)

items.summary: Base vacuity runs are never retried alone. If a new criterion's base run fails only because of contention with concurrent runs (shared DB, port or temp file), the criterion counts as non-vacuous and a vacuous criterion can pass. The solo retry covers only head failures. Consider re-running an overlapped base failure alone too, or documenting this asymmetry in SPEC §6.3.

Total process concurrency is run.verify_parallel × verify.check_parallel. With both on 'auto' that is about floor(cpus/8) × floor(cpus/4); on 32 CPUs, 4 verifies × 8 checks = 32 concurrent check processes plus test_count runs. The contract does not bound or document this combined load.
items.resolution_reason: Combined concurrency is bounded by CPU-based auto limits; documentation nit

items.summary: `baseDir` is assigned before `git worktree add` completes. If the add fails, the finally block runs `worktree remove --force` on a path that is not a worktree and ignores the result. This is harmless because rmSync and prune follow, but the add failure is reported only through gitOk's error and the cleanup errors are silent. This behaviour existed before F26.

The AC-1 and ES-2 tests depend on wall-clock timing (1000 ms sleeps, a 2 s timeout, and startup overlap). On a heavily loaded CI host, maxOverlap could fall below the limit and the tests could flake. Consider synchronization barriers, as fbbfe32 did for F25 AC-3.

Interactive `harness eval` computes independence with conflict=false, so a builder conflict_model used in an earlier run round is not counted. Only `harness run` passes the actual builder models via `builders`.
items.resolution_reason: Interactive eval cannot know whether a conflict model was used; low-impact independence label (evidence: lib/adapters/index.mjs:79 builderModels conflict=false default)

items.summary: lib/eval.mjs defaultRunAdapter still calls resolveRole and falls back to it when opts.model is undefined. This is redundant now that evaluate always passes a model, and a null model is not distinguished from 'unset'.
items.resolution_reason: Redundant fallback, harmless (evidence: lib/eval.mjs:487-495)

items.summary: The unit test of the doctor warning and the AC-5 block-shape regexes depend on exact padding and label text such as 'escalate (r≥2)'. They are brittle to cosmetic output changes.
items.resolution_reason: Test-style brittleness only

items.summary: SPEC §10 says model values are "checked again right before adapter arguments", but the re-check lives only in roleModel(). The adapter buildArgs (claude/codex/gemini) and eval.mjs defaultRunAdapter's resolveRole fallback do not check the value themselves. Every current path goes through validated config (validateUser runs in loadConfig, and in runFeatures for both fresh and resumed runs) or through roleModel, so no bypass exists today. Moving isSafeModel into buildArgs would make this defence-in-depth claim hold for future callers.
items.resolution_reason: Defence-in-depth only; all paths validated today (evidence: lib/adapters/index.mjs:69)

items.summary: Doctor's policyOf reads spec.escalate and spec.conflict_model directly and not through roleModel. This is safe because the config is validated first, but the builder's escalate and conflict display lines follow a different code path from the tier lines.
items.resolution_reason: Safe after validation; code-path consistency nit (evidence: lib/commands/doctor.mjs:19-26)

items.summary: Redaction (SC-1) only replaces literal values of 8 or more characters taken from the run's env. A secret that is shorter, transformed (base64, URL-encoded, split across lines) or absent from the env would still reach the report. The 8-character cutoff is documented in SPEC §8.
items.resolution_reason: Documented design limit of env-value redaction (SPEC §8, MIN_SECRET) (evidence: lib/failures.mjs:8)

items.summary: Missing commands are recognised only by exit code (127 or 9009), the shell's 'not recognized' text, or ENOENT. A feature script or verify command that itself exits 127 for its own reasons is treated as an environment stop instead of a round failure. The run then stops on every --resume rather than blocking.

The Windows paths (exit 9009 and the cmd.exe 'is not recognized' line) are covered only by a missingProgram unit test on fake stderr. No end-to-end test exercises them, since the fixtures run on POSIX.
items.resolution_reason: Windows e2e coverage gap; unit test covers detection

items.summary: An environment stop caused by a missing program in the vacuity (base) run of a criterion check is not distinguished. Only head check results, verify commands and test_count feed environmentFailure.

The `- failed:` lines are derived from the last verify of the round and kept in e.verifyFailures. A feature blocked for a non-verify reason (for example stall after an evaluator failure) can carry failure items from an earlier failed attempt. This matches the SPEC wording but may be noisy.
items.resolution_reason: Matches SPEC wording; possible noise only

items.summary: Redaction runs after verify.mjs has already cut the output with tail() to the last 2000 characters. If the cut falls inside a secret value, the remaining suffix no longer matches the full value, so it is not redacted. It then appears near the start of the 300-character report message. Example: with SECRET_TOKEN=sk-abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz0123456789 and output = value + 1990 'x' characters, the report shows '0123456789xxx…'. Commands run with a filtered env, so this needs the secret to reach the output some other way (for example, read from a file). Fix idea: redact before tail(), or also redact a leading partial match of each value.

Only report messages are redacted. The state file .harness/runs/current.json still stores e.lastVerify, whose command output is unredacted, and the blocked post_merge_verify `detail` uses v.error unredacted. Both behaved this way before F29 and SC-1 covers only the report's failure messages, but the redaction is not applied consistently.
The redactor skips values shorter than 8 characters, so short secrets (such as PINs) outside env_allowlist are never redacted. This is documented in SPEC §8, but it is a deliberate gap.
items.resolution_reason: Same 8-char redaction cutoff limitation (same as B191) (evidence: B191)

items.summary: F29 blocked (post_merge_verify): verify failed on the integration branch after the merge — verify failed on the merged integration branch; merge rolled back

options.summary: split F29 so the feature ship as a separate feature with its own contract
rewrite the criteria for the feature (new contract version, re-approval)
accept the risk: drop or relax the feature with a recorded decision

items.resolution_reason: rescope for F29; feature passed (evidence: .harness/features.json F29 passed)

items.summary: The unit test for the CLI message in AC-1 only greps the source of lib/commands/run.mjs for strings. It does not run the CLI. ES-1 does run the CLI, so the message path is covered end to end, but the AC-1 test itself is weak.
items.resolution_reason: Weak unit test but ES-1 covers path end to end

items.summary: A --resume run that finds the program missing again at the post-merge verify stage repeats the merge and rollback each time. It is correct and consumes no round, but the merge work is redone on every resume.
items.resolution_reason: Correct, only redundant work on resume

items.summary: A parallel run stopped by an environment failure leaves other features paused via Paused. If one of them hits a different fatal error in its current step, that error replaces the environment stop as the run's failure, so the environment reason is not reported. This edge case is not tested.
items.resolution_reason: Rare untested edge in error reporting precedence

items.summary: The redactor matches allowlist keys case-sensitively. On Windows, env keys are case-insensitive, so a differently-cased allowlisted name (e.g. 'path' vs 'PATH') would have its value redacted. This garbles the text but does not leak anything.
items.resolution_reason: Windows case variants of common keys are in the allowlist; remaining mismatch only garbles text, no leak (evidence: lib/exec.mjs:8-13)

items.summary: The failed item (the verify command string) is written to the report without redaction. It comes from config, not from the env, so it only leaks if a user writes a secret literally into verify.commands.
items.resolution_reason: Report and verdict are rendered from redacted data; the item field is not in the keep-list (evidence: lib/run.mjs:1562 renderReport(redactDeep(state,...)); lib/eval.mjs:714)

items.summary: The base count cache is keyed by (merge-base sha, command string, rule) only. A command whose output depends on the environment (tool versions, env vars, config outside git) reuses a stale cached base count. Nothing invalidates the entry, and the file is a plain writable JSON, so a wrong value only goes away when the key changes or the entry is overwritten.
items.resolution_reason: Cache keyed by merge-base/command/rule by design; env-dependent counts are out of scope

items.summary: For from:commands[i] the base run ignores the exit code, so a base run that crashes after printing a partial '# tests N' summary line is cached as the base count. That can under-state base and hide a later decrease.
items.resolution_reason: Theoretical: a crash after printing a summary line; summary lines are printed at the end (evidence: lib/verify.mjs:142-151)

items.summary: Concurrent verifies re-read the cache file and then write it atomically, but there is no lock. Two verifies finishing at the same moment can drop each other's entry. The cost is only an extra base run later.
items.resolution_reason: Lost cache entry only costs an extra base run

items.summary: The F30 test file takes about 43 s because each case builds a git fixture and runs real subprocesses. Several tests assert exact run counts through log files, which is robust, but the file is slow on loaded CI.
items.resolution_reason: Test speed preference

items.summary: The cache trusts any valid non-negative integer. SC-1 rejects only strings, negatives, fractions and null. If an entry for the current (merge-base, command, rule) key holds a smaller valid integer such as 0, it is used as the base count and a real test decrease is reported as ok. The cache lives at paths(root).runs, and when verify runs in a feature worktree that path is under the builder's worktree; runs/** is also exempt from the .harness integrity check. A cooperative builder is unlikely to write this file (threat model D1), but the cache has no provenance check such as core-only storage outside the worktree or a keyed checksum.
items.resolution_reason: Run verifies with root = main checkout, so the cache lives outside the builder worktree; tampering would also be D1 (evidence: lib/run.mjs:948 root, lib/verify.mjs:498)

items.summary: .harness/runs/test-count-cache.json is not gitignored (git check-ignore finds no rule for it). A core or builder `git add -A` in a feature worktree could commit the cache into the feature branch and then into integration. Entries are keyed by commit sha, so stale entries are harmless, but the file would grow in history and carry cache state between checkouts.
items.resolution_reason: init gitignores the cache and builder commit excludes it (evidence: lib/commands/init.mjs:30; lib/run.mjs:978)

items.summary: storeCount rereads the file and then writes it atomically without a lock. When verifies of different features run in parallel against a shared root, one write can overwrite another's entry (last writer wins). The only effect is an extra base run later, not a wrong count.
items.resolution_reason: Same unlocked cache write race (same as B207) (evidence: B207)

items.summary: lib/commands/approve.mjs runs `git config user.email` with spawnSync and no timeout, so it is not bounded by budget.git_timeout_sec. It is not a verify/eval/run git call, so it is outside AC-1.
items.resolution_reason: git config user.email reads local config, practically never hangs; outside AC scope (evidence: lib/commands/approve.mjs:31)

items.summary: In verify.mjs the cleanup `git worktree remove` and `git worktree prune` sit in a finally block. They now throw HarnessError(git) on timeout, and that error can replace the original error from the try body. The remove and prune calls are also not wrapped, unlike the earlier best-effort handling (see B184).
items.resolution_reason: Cleanup worktree remove/prune are wrapped in try/catch (evidence: lib/verify.mjs:617-626)

items.summary: runFeatures fills the shared `gitOpts` object with timeoutSec only after the config is validated. Any core git call made before that point would use the default 300s instead of the configured value. No such call exists today, but the ordering is implicit.
items.resolution_reason: Implicit ordering; no git call precedes validation (evidence: lib/run.mjs:689-690)

items.summary: The SC-1 and AC-3 tests use wall-clock budgets (5s and 15s) with a fake git that sleeps for 30s or more. They can be slow on a loaded machine. This is similar to B177 and B185.

items.summary: lib/run.mjs integration merge (around line 851): a `git merge` that times out now throws instead of returning a failed result. As a result, the `merge --abort` path is never reached. The integration worktree can be left mid-merge (MERGE_HEAD present) until the next run or a manual cleanup. This only happens when a merge takes longer than budget.git_timeout_sec (300s by default).
items.resolution_reason: Rare (merge > git_timeout_sec); next run refuses the dirty integration worktree with a clear message (evidence: lib/run.mjs:990-991)

items.summary: In lib/eval.mjs, git() reads `opts.timeoutSec` without optional chaining, while the line above uses `opts?.signal`. Every current caller passes opts, so nothing fails today. A future caller that omits opts and hits a timeout would get a TypeError instead of the git timeout error.
items.resolution_reason: Every caller passes opts; hypothetical future caller (evidence: lib/eval.mjs:208)

items.summary: validateUser accepts any finite positive budget.git_timeout_sec. Values above about 2147483.647 s (2^31-1 ms) overflow Node's setTimeout, which then fires after 1 ms, so every core git command would 'time out' at once. Consider an upper bound in validation. step_timeout_sec probably has the same issue.

Core git helpers now throw on timeout. When a git call in a cleanup path (for example verify's finally that runs `worktree remove --force` for the base worktree) times out, the new HarnessError(git) may replace the original error or result that was being reported. Previously a timed-out cleanup returned a result that the caller ignored.
items.resolution_reason: Cleanup git timeout replacing original error (now caught) (same as B213) (evidence: B213)

items.resolution_reason: gitOpts timeout set after validation (same as B214) (evidence: B214)

items.resolution_reason: Field kept only for pre-F32 state migration (evidence: lib/run.mjs:1235)

items.summary: failedTestNames trims leading whitespace before matching '✖ ' / 'not ok ', so indented nested failures count. This is broader than the contract's literal 'lines starting with'; it is documented in SPEC §6.1 and docs/run.md but is a deliberate extension.
items.resolution_reason: Deliberate documented extension (SPEC §6.1)

items.summary: flaky_tests names come from raw command output and are not passed through the env-value redactor before they go into the verdict and the run report, unlike verify_failures messages.
items.resolution_reason: Verdict record including flaky_tests goes through redactDeep; run state and report are redacted too (evidence: lib/eval.mjs:713-714; lib/run.mjs:710,1562)

A test name that contains an env secret value (for example a parametrized test title) would appear unredacted.
items.resolution_reason: flaky_tests redaction (now redacted) (same as B238) (evidence: B238)

items.summary: The base-side vacuity limit only applies to `verify.vacuity_timeout_sec` inside `verify()`. `run --resume` state files written before F33 have no `vacuity_timeout_sec`, so they fall back to DEFAULTS through `?? DEFAULTS.verify.vacuity_timeout_sec`. That is correct, but no test covers a resumed snapshot without the key.
items.resolution_reason: Resume fallback to DEFAULTS is correct; test gap only

items.summary: A base run that times out is treated as non-vacuous. A criterion whose check hangs on base for reasons unrelated to the feature therefore skips the vacuity guarantee, and only `base_timed_out: true` in the result records this. This follows the contract, but nothing in the verify output or the eval prompt surfaces the flag to a human or the evaluator.
items.resolution_reason: A base timeout now adds a warning to verify output (evidence: lib/verify.mjs:563-566)

items.summary: A base timeout now counts as 'did not pass on base'. A check that really passes on base but takes longer than vacuity_timeout_sec (default 120s, e.g. a slow full test suite) is therefore reported as non-vacuous, and a vacuous criterion can pass. The contract (AC-2) and SPEC §6.3 specify this behaviour. Consider adding a warning line to the verify output when base_timed_out is set, so a reviewer can notice it.

verify.vacuity_timeout_sec accepts any positive number, including very small ones such as 0.001. With such a value every base vacuity run times out, which in effect turns off the vacuity check for all new criteria without any warning. Consider a minimum value, or a doctor or verify warning for values below a few seconds.
items.resolution_reason: User-chosen value; base limit is max(vacuity_timeout_sec, 3x head time) so tiny values no longer disable vacuity for real checks (evidence: docs/SPEC.md:103)

items.resolution_reason: An aborted run stops the whole run; the verdict of that verify is not used

items.summary: KEEP_UNREDACTED in lib/run.mjs is matched by key name at any depth (e.g. 'files', 'title', 'feature', 'history', 'config'). A future nested field with one of those names that holds command output would be saved unredacted. Today none of the verify or state shapes do. Consider limiting the keep-list to top-level paths of the state and result entries.
items.resolution_reason: Key-name keep-list is hypothetical risk for future fields; eval keep-list already narrowed to feature/contract_hash (evidence: lib/run.mjs:79; lib/eval.mjs:721)

For example, lastVerify.cwd can be saved as '[redacted]/.harness/wt/F34'. Nothing reads these fields back on --resume, so this is only cosmetic, but it can hamper debugging of a saved state.

items.summary: The F34 tests write records with an injected env, but there is no test for the interactive `harness eval` command, which uses the default env = process.env. The default path is a one-line default parameter, so the risk is low.
items.resolution_reason: One-line default parameter; low risk

No path puts command output under those keys today, but a future field with one of those names would silently skip redaction. Consider scoping the exemption to known paths.
items.resolution_reason: Key-name KEEP_UNREDACTED (same as B248) (evidence: B248)

items.summary: KEEP_UNREDACTED in lib/run.mjs and lib/eval.mjs exempts keys by name at any depth (e.g. 'files', 'title', 'feature', 'history', 'config'). Today no command output is stored under those keys, but a future field with one of those names would silently skip redaction. The 'config' snapshot is also saved verbatim, so a secret placed in the config (for example an adapter command line) is not redacted.
items.resolution_reason: Key-name KEEP_UNREDACTED (eval part already narrowed) (same as B248) (evidence: B248)

Resume-critical fields are exempt, and the F34 tests resume successfully with a real process.env. Any future state field that stores an absolute path outside the exempt list would be garbled when PWD is a prefix of it.

items.resolution_reason: Metrics lines are redacted except grouping keys (evidence: lib/metrics.mjs:39-42; lib/run.mjs:719)

items.resolution_reason: Return value differs but nothing leaks (file written redacted) (evidence: lib/eval.mjs:736-737)

items.summary: In the builder-changes commit, the pathspec `:(exclude,literal)<cache>` only leaves out the test-count cache. If a project already tracks that file, its modifications stay unstaged after the commit and the feature worktree is left dirty. The cache is now gitignored by `harness init`, but projects initialised earlier have no such entry.
items.resolution_reason: Run keeps the cache under the main checkout (root), never in the feature worktree, so a tracked cache is not modified there; commit also excludes it (evidence: lib/run.mjs:948,978; lib/verify.mjs:498)

items.summary: The solo base re-run loop at the end of verify runs `runCommand` directly and does not go through the pool or check for an abort signal. A SIGINT during that phase is only noticed by whatever runs next. The same gap exists for the head solo re-run loop.
items.resolution_reason: Solo re-run loops do not check abort signal (same as B261) (evidence: B261)

items.summary: The AC-1, AC-2 and ES-1 tests use wall-clock polling: a 3 s wait for another run to be seen, an 8 s hang, and 5 s vacuity timeouts. They could be flaky on a heavily loaded CI host, as with B185 and B177.
items.resolution_reason: Wall-clock test timing; no observed flake

items.summary: If .harness/runs/test-count-cache.json is already tracked on the base (it was committed before 3be2b83), the builder-commit pathspec exclude leaves its modification unstaged. The feature worktree then stays dirty after the builder commit, and nothing reports it. Consider `git rm --cached` or a warning when the cache is tracked.
items.resolution_reason: Tracked cache leaving worktree dirty (same as B257) (evidence: B257)

items.summary: The solo base re-run loop runs after the head retry loop but does not check the abort signal between iterations. A SIGINT during a long series of solo base re-runs relies on runCommand's own signal handling (via `run`), and every queued re-run is still started in turn.
items.resolution_reason: Aborted signal kills each started command immediately (pre-aborted signal handled); only a few extra instant spawns (evidence: lib/exec.mjs:87)

items.summary: The AC-3 test returns early on Windows (the fake git is a shebang script), so the failed-worktree-add cleanup path is exercised only on POSIX.
items.resolution_reason: Windows e2e coverage gap

items.summary: The fragment rule applies to every string in the recorded files, not only to cut command output. Any string of 8 or more characters that starts with a suffix of a non-allowlisted env value, or ends with a prefix of one, is replaced by '[redacted]'. Examples are a path fragment or a title-like string. This matches SPEC SR-9 but can garble unrelated short strings when env values are path-like.
items.resolution_reason: Matches SPEC SR-9 by design

items.summary: `harness verify` (lib/commands/verify.mjs) still calls verify() without a redactor. Its terminal output is not one of the five record paths, so it stays unredacted. It would matter if that output were ever piped into a record.
items.resolution_reason: Terminal output of harness verify is not a record

items.summary: exec.mjs caps the captured output to its tail before verify redacts it. A cut at that earlier cap is only handled by the leading-fragment rule, which needs 8 or more characters of the value. That is acceptable under SR-9 but is not tested.
items.resolution_reason: Accepted under SR-9; test gap only

items.summary: The metrics redaction keeps only feature, step, started_at and ended_at. The role, adapter, model and outcome strings are also passed through the redactor, which is harmless but slightly wider than needed.
items.resolution_reason: Harmless over-redaction

items.summary: The redaction of adapter-error text ('crashed [redacted]') is tested only with a leading fragment of the secret that keeps its ending. The trailing-fragment path through metrics, backlog and verdict is covered only by redactor unit tests, not by end-to-end fixtures.
items.resolution_reason: Test coverage gap; unit tests cover the path

items.summary: Adapter error detail is cut by tail() in lib/adapters/common.mjs:175 and then placed in the middle of a string, e.g. run.mjs:1031 `builder ${error} (${detail})` or 966. A fragment of a secret at the cut ends up mid-string, so the edge-fragment rule never sees it and it can reach the state file, report or backlog. SPEC SR-9 explicitly puts mid-string fragments out of scope. Consider redacting `detail` before it is embedded, or redacting in the adapter before tail().

A string that is entirely an inner slice of a secret (both edges cut, e.g. S.slice(3,30)) is not redacted, because it is neither a prefix nor a suffix of the value. The current verify paths do not produce this, since they redact before cutting. SR-9 documents it as out of scope.
items.resolution_reason: Documented out of scope in SR-9; no current path produces an inner slice

items.summary: trailingFragment only matches when the string ends exactly on the prefix. A prefix fragment followed by a trailing newline or whitespace ('head sk-abcdefgh\n') is not redacted, while leadingFragment does handle 'fragment...\r\n' at the start. There is no current path that produces this, because start-cuts happen after redaction.
items.resolution_reason: No current path produces it (cuts happen after redaction); theoretical

items.summary: evalAndRecord builds its metrics redactor from process.env, while evaluate() redacts the verdict with its own `env` parameter. The two coincide in production, but a caller that passes a custom env gets metrics redacted against a different value set.
items.resolution_reason: evalAndRecord takes no env param and evaluate() is called without env, so both use process.env; theoretical (evidence: lib/eval-status.mjs:162-166)

items.summary: The F37 timing tests (head 5s, base 6s, several 20s bounded waits) rely on wall-clock time and process startup, so they may flake or run slowly on a loaded CI host. Similar to B177 and B185.
items.resolution_reason: Wall-clock test flakiness under load; F46 (load stability) was accepted as a risk

items.summary: In the base-retry path, the base solo re-run reuses the limit stored from the first base run (baseRetry map). This matches the SPEC, but no test covers the combination of overlapped-then-retried with a base timeout.
items.resolution_reason: Test-coverage gap for an edge combination; behaviour matches SPEC

items.summary: The head duration used for the base limit is measured inside pool(), so time spent waiting in the queue is not counted. Contention from concurrent runs can still make the head run longer, which only makes the base limit more generous. It never makes it shorter, so vacuity detection is not weakened. Not documented in SPEC §6.3.
items.resolution_reason: Only makes the base limit more generous; no weakening of vacuity detection

items.summary: The F37 tests depend on wall-clock timing (head runs of 2–5 s, base runs of 6–20 s, the 3× multiplier) and take about 85 s. Under heavy CI load, node startup time could push a 'fast' head run above 2 s, raising the limit past 6 s and flaking the exact base_timeout_sec === 6 assertions.
items.resolution_reason: Wall-clock flakiness of F37 tests; F46 load stability accepted as risk

items.summary: leaveMerge does not clean untracked files. If merge --abort fails, a builder-created untracked file stays in the worktree after the reset. The blocked detail says the worktree was reset, which could suggest it is fully clean.
items.resolution_reason: Only after merge --abort fails (rare); untracked leftover is harmless and reset is reported

items.summary: A resolve run whose merge completed cleanly stores snapshot=null, so every path that differs from the pre-merge HEAD counts as changed. This is harmless today because no builder runs in that case (B161). Documenting it, or an explicit test, would make the invariant less implicit.
items.resolution_reason: Harmless invariant (no builder runs when merge was clean); documentation nit

items.summary: The AC-3 test's no-overlap assertion depends on a 60 ms sleep. It works, but on a loaded host the timing could make it flaky (see B177/B185).
items.resolution_reason: 60 ms sleep timing test; load flakiness accepted with F46

items.summary: leaveMerge acts only when MERGE_HEAD exists. If the conflict-resolution builder commits the merge itself and a marker check fails afterwards, fail() leaves the feature worktree on that merge commit, with the markers in it, and never resets to preMergeHead. The integration branch is unaffected. Consider resetting to e.conflict.preMergeHead when HEAD has moved.

The comment above gitLock in lib/run.mjs (~line 596) still reads 'Worktree, branch and merge changes go through one lock'. It does not mention the add/commit/reset --hard calls that isSerializedGit now serializes.
items.resolution_reason: Comment wording nit; isSerializedGit docstring already lists add/commit/reset --hard (evidence: lib/run.mjs:143-147)

items.summary: The iac profile's verify command is the bare string 'harness tf-check'. In target projects where harness is not on PATH (CLAUDE.md suggests `npx github:hanbyeol/cc-harness`), verify fails with 'command not found: harness', which makes it an environment stop. The docs do not tell iac users that harness must be on PATH, and they do not say how to override the command (e.g. `npx ... tf-check`).

tf-check runs terraform subcommands with runCommand's default 1800 s timeout for each call, independent of the outer verify step timeout. A hanging init in one directory can use up the whole step budget, and the per-call timeout is neither documented nor configurable.
items.resolution_reason: Outer verify step timeout still bounds the whole command; per-call default is a doc nit

items.summary: Validate and fmt error output is printed in full, while init errors are truncated to 300 characters. Validate output on a large module can be long. This is consistent with the contract but asymmetric.
items.resolution_reason: Asymmetric truncation, consistent with contract; low value

items.summary: The provider-cache test on Linux relies on XDG_CACHE_HOME. The docs note that verify's filtered env drops XDG_CACHE_HOME, so the path used inside verify differs from the one used by a direct CLI call. This is documented but may surprise users.
items.resolution_reason: Documented behaviour

items.summary: The AC-2 criterion text writes the brief format as 'todo N (v1 partial P · blocked B)'. The implementation keeps the existing 'N todo' order, giving 'N todo (v1 partial P · blocked B)', and SPEC §13 and README use that order too. The contract wording and the output differ only in word order, so the contract text could be aligned in a later version.
items.resolution_reason: Contract wording vs output word order; wording nit

items.resolution_reason: Follows contract; design preference

items.summary: stress.mjs discards child stderr (child.stderr.resume()). A crash that prints only to stderr is reported only as '<test runner exited N without a failing test>', with no diagnostic text.
lint-contract rule 3 flags the technical term '절대 경로' (absolute path) as the universal '절대(로)'; contracts must rephrase it (seen in F42 SC-1).

The continuation prompt lists every changed path with no cap on count or length. A timed-out build that left many untracked files (for example an installed node_modules or build output that is not gitignored) would make the list large. Paths are also inserted verbatim, so a path with a newline could alter the prompt layout. Consider capping the list and escaping unusual characters.

changedFromBase counts any file under .harness/ or generated artifacts as 'changes'. A timed-out build that only produced such files would still be continued instead of blocked(budget). The SPEC says 'any change against base', so this is consistent, but it may continue on non-progress.
items.resolution_reason: Consistent with SPEC "any change against base"; attempt cap bounds it

items.summary: The continuation note does not tell the builder which attempt number it is or that the next timeout can block. The builder cannot budget its remaining time or attempts.
items.resolution_reason: Prompt header already gives the attempt number; max-attempt hint is a nice-to-have (evidence: lib/run.mjs:317)

items.summary: Continuation prompt lists changed file paths verbatim, one per '- ' line. A path created by the builder that contains newlines or markdown/prompt-like text (git -z output keeps it unquoted) is injected into the next builder prompt as-is. The builder only reaches its own session, so under threat model D1 this is not a trust-boundary crossing, but escaping or JSON-quoting the paths would make the list unambiguous.
items.resolution_reason: Builder-created path only reaches its own session (threat model D1); quoting is folded into the B298 fix

items.summary: The continuation file list is unbounded. A timed-out build that generated thousands of files (e.g. an untracked node_modules or build output that isn't gitignored) puts every path in the next prompt, which can blow the prompt size or cost. Consider capping the list and adding a '… N more' line.
items.resolution_reason: duplicate of B298: unbounded continuation file list

items.summary: e.continuation.files is saved unredacted in run state because 'files' is in KEEP_UNREDACTED. Paths are not command output, so this matches the intent, but a secret in a file name would persist to the state file and the prompt. That is outside SC-1, which covers file contents and env values only.
items.resolution_reason: File names are not command output; secret-in-filename is out of SC-1 scope and negligible

items.summary: The SC-1 test checks only a file whose content is a secret and the env var API_TOKEN. It does not cover a continuation across a committed file together with staged edits, or a rename entry. Code review shows dirtyPaths handles R/C source tokens correctly, but no test exercises a rename in the continuation list.
items.resolution_reason: Test gap only; code review shows renames handled

items.summary: The F16 vacuity-overlay tests now run their new test files through a `run.mjs` runner, because the F42 rule stops a `node test/x.test.mjs` check from getting its new entry file on base. Assertions are unchanged, but the fixtures no longer exercise the direct-entry shape for F16. F42 AC-1 and AC-2 cover that shape, so this is only worth a look for `assert-count` review.
items.resolution_reason: Intentional fixture change; direct-entry shape covered by F42 tests

items.summary: `isNotFound` is skipped for every criterion that has `base_entry`, not only for the withheld file's own 127 exit. A missing interpreter such as `python3` absent on base, or a command-not-found from inside the entry, is therefore treated as an ordinary base failure and not as a `base_not_found` environment stop. The check still ends up non-vacuous, but the environment signal is lost.
items.resolution_reason: A missing interpreter on base would also be missing on head (same env), so the lost signal is theoretical

items.summary: `checkEntry` returns null for a check that starts with an env assignment (`FOO=1 node test/x.mjs`), `cd sub && node …` or `node -- path`. Such checks keep the old overlay behaviour, so they stay vacuous. This matches the documented scope, but the docs could list these shapes.
items.resolution_reason: Documented scope of checkEntry; fails safe (old overlay behaviour)

items.summary: Each distinct withheld entry creates one more base worktree (a `git worktree add` plus an overlay copy). A contract with many new-entry criteria multiplies that cost, and worktrees are only created serially inside the criterion runs.
items.resolution_reason: duplicate of B311: unbounded per-entry base worktrees

items.summary: The base vacuity runs execute with cwd set to the base worktree top level, while head checks run in the project directory (root). In a monorepo subdirectory project, checkEntry's path is normalized relative to the base top, but the overlay paths carry the projectRel prefix. As a result, a relative entry such as 'node test/tool.mjs' never matches 'pkg/app/test/tool.mjs', and the rule silently doesn't apply. This is conservative (the entry is overlaid as before), and the head/base cwd mismatch predates F42, but the SPEC wording ('base worktree 최상위 기준') leaves monorepo projects without the new rule.
items.resolution_reason: Monorepo-subdirectory case fails safe to the old overlay behaviour; predates F42

items.summary: On case-insensitive filesystems (macOS/Windows), a check such as 'node Test/tool.mjs' runs the new test/tool.mjs on head, but checkEntry returns 'Test/tool.mjs', which does not match the overlay set. The file is then overlaid, and the criterion may be judged vacuous as before. This errs on the conservative side, and no test covers it.
items.resolution_reason: Case-mismatched path errs conservative; rare

items.summary: Each distinct withheld entry creates an additional base git worktree, and there is no upper bound. A contract with many new criteria that each use a different new entry script creates that many worktrees (disk/time cost). They are cleaned up in finally.
items.resolution_reason: One base worktree per distinct new entry script is bounded by contract size and cleaned in finally; cost only

items.summary: The F16 overlay tests were changed from 'node test/math.test.mjs' to 'node run.mjs test/math.test.mjs' so they keep exercising the overlay under the new entry rule. The assertions are unchanged, but the original direct-entry shape is no longer covered by F16. That shape is now covered by F42 AC-1 with the opposite expected outcome, which is intended by the contract.
items.resolution_reason: duplicate of B305: F16 fixtures rewritten to run.mjs

items.summary: checkEntry only recognises a check whose first word is the runner. Leading env assignments (`FOO=1 node test/tool.mjs`) and `cd x && node ...` get no entry rule, so a new entry script run this way is still overlaid on base and can be judged vacuous. The contract excludes second commands, but the env-prefix form is not documented as unsupported.
items.resolution_reason: duplicate of B307: checkEntry ignores env-prefix / cd shapes

items.summary: Each distinct withheld entry creates one more base git worktree (addBaseWorktree plus a full overlay). A contract with many new-tool criteria adds worktree setup cost, and the worktrees are created lazily and cleaned up only at the end of verify.
items.resolution_reason: duplicate of B311: per-entry base worktree cost

items.summary: F16 vacuity tests were rewritten to route through a base-side runner (`run.mjs`) so the new-test-file overlay still applies. This is necessary under the new rule, but it changes the shape of the existing F16 fixtures. The original direct `node test/math.test.mjs` shape is now covered only by the F42 tests.
items.resolution_reason: duplicate of B305: F16 fixtures rewritten to run.mjs

items.summary: checkEntry resolves the entry path relative to where the check runs, but overlay/newOnBase paths are relative to the git top. When the project (.harness dir) is a subdirectory of the repository, the two can differ and the entry rule silently does not apply (fails safe: the old behaviour). This is not described or tested.

items.summary: checkEntry normalizes 'node test/x/..' to 'test', a directory. It is harmless because it never matches an overlaid file, but the parser could reject paths that normalize to a directory-like result.
items.resolution_reason: Harmless: a directory result never matches an overlaid file

items.summary: A separate base worktree is created for each distinct withheld entry. A contract with many new-entry criteria multiplies worktree creation and disk use, and nothing bounds it.
items.resolution_reason: duplicate of B311: per-entry base worktree cost

items.summary: expandFileGlob uses fs.globSync. It exists from Node 22.0 but is experimental there, so on Node 22/23 every --files run prints an ExperimentalWarning to stderr. It is harmless, but it is noise in stress output.
items.resolution_reason: Only on Node 22/23 and only in the stress test tool; harmless warning

items.summary: AC-2 passes without any change to the F23/F25/F26/F28 test files. items.summary: firstProgram splits words with a regex that does not handle a quoted VAR assignment value containing a space. For `FOO="a b" jest` it picks `b"` as the program, so a genuine 127 from jest is judged a plain failure. This is a rare edge case.
items.resolution_reason: firstProgram now handles a quoted VAR value with a space (evidence: lib/exec.mjs:122-127 (firstProgram(`FOO="a b" jest`) === "jest"))

items.summary: builtinInvocation runs the core's bin/harness.mjs, so any `harness <args>` command bypasses a user-installed harness of a different version. The behaviour is intentional, but a project pinning another harness version via PATH gets the core's version in verify. Consider documenting this.

items.summary: builtinInvocation allows '%' in plain words. Because the built-in path spawns node without a shell, a word such as '%PATH%' is passed literally. The shell path would expand it on Windows, so the same command string can mean different things depending on which path runs it. This is not a security issue, since running without a shell is the safer side, but SPEC §6.1 could say that no variable expansion happens in built-in mode.
items.resolution_reason: builtinInvocation no longer accepts % in plain words; such commands go to the shell (evidence: lib/exec.mjs:148 PLAIN_WORD excludes %)

items.summary: The built-in 'harness ' execution also applies to commands other than tf-check (for example 'harness verify F1' or 'harness run' as a check). A check can therefore re-enter the core recursively with this checkout's version, not the version on PATH. The contract permits this, but the SPEC does not say that the PATH version is ignored for every subcommand.
items.resolution_reason: duplicate of B324: built-in harness path ignores the PATH version

items.summary: presetCount passes preset.bin, a bare program name rather than a command line, to isCommandNotFound. This works because firstProgram returns the name itself, but it relies on preset names never containing spaces or '=' prefixes.

items.summary: The new 127 rule looks only at the command's first program. This follows the SPEC wording, but users of chained commands lose the environment-stop behaviour.

items.summary: The new first-program 127 rule classifies compound commands such as 'cd sub && make' (with make missing) as a plain failure, because the first program is 'cd'. items.summary: commandNotFound matches only the command line's first word. items.summary: The `harness tf-check` not-found message now begins with `harness tf-check:` so it passes the first-program rule. items.summary: The F37 tests were rewritten to use a TOOL file placed in the worktree and `.` on PATH, instead of the old probe script that exited 127 from inside a script. items.summary: conflictMarkedFiles only lstats the last path component.
